title: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — Paul adds ἄχρι νόμου; Calvin: the doubt was only before the law
pass_a_gloss: A second proof: Paul does not merely say sin was in the world; he adds ἄχρι νόμου. He means Moses’ law (v.20: the law entered that sin might abound), and next says μέχρι Μωϋσέως. Why ‘until the law’ not ‘until Moses’? Calvin: one could doubt whether there was sin before the law; after the law it was undoubted—the question stuck only on the pre-law time. Enough, then, to prove sin from Adam to the law.
pass_b_english: To this argument let another be added, drawn from this: that the Apostle does not simply say sin was in the world, but adds ἄχρι νόμου, until the law.
And he no doubt means the law of Moses, which in verse 20 he teaches entered besides, that sin might abound.
And so in place of ἄχρι νόμου he said in the following verse μέχρι Μωϋσέως, until Moses.
But why did the Apostle use ‘until the law,’ not ‘until Moses’?
Namely, to use Calvin’s words, it could be doubted whether there was sin in the world before the law.
That there was after the law was not at all doubtful.
The question stuck only on the time preceding the law.
It was therefore enough to prove that sin was in the world from Adam until the law.
source_text: Huic argumento accedat alterum hinc petitum, quod Apostolus non simpliciter dicit peccatum fuisse in mundo, sed addit ἄχρι νόμου, usque ad legem. Intelligit autem proculdubio legem Mosis, quam versu 20. praeterea ingressam ut abundaret peccatum docet. Itaque loco ἄχρι νόμου dixit versu sequente μέχρι Μωϋσέως, usque ad Mosen. Cur autem Apostolus illud usurpaviti usque ad legem, non usque ad Mosen? Nempe, ut verbis utar Calvini, dubitari poterat anne ante legem esset peccatum in mundo. Post legem fuisse minime dubium erat. Tantum haerebat quaestio in tempore legem praecedente. Satis igitur fuit probare peccatum fuisse in mundo ab Adam usque ad legem.

choices.choice: Paul targets the doubted pre-law span (Calvin)
